row.basis: few of noble birth among the called
row.note: Paul says the called include few people of noble birth; this directly tests the commentary's noble lineage against the community formed by faith.
Paul says God chooses what the world calls weak; the commentary's hanâsir are weak people, yet weakness does not determine their worth before God.

row.basis: God chooses the low and despised
row.note: Paul's low and despised are chosen to overturn what claims standing; this closely matches the commentary's lowest freedmen and its reversal of rank.

row.basis: no flesh may boast before God
row.note: Paul gives the aim of the preceding choice of low people: no human may boast before God; inherited rank cannot ground superiority.
A richly dressed visitor receives a good seat while a poor visitor is told to stand or sit below; the congregation enacts exactly the rank division questioned in the commentary.
James says God chose the poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom; faith overturns the low social rank assigned to the weak.
James reproaches believers for dishonoring the poor while the rich oppress them; this supplies the social action behind calling the lowly inferior.
Mary's song says God brings rulers down from thrones and lifts the humble; the commentary likewise sets divine standing against human rank.
The hungry receive good things while the rich leave empty; this gives material force to the commentary's pairing of the weak and low with a reversal of value.

row.basis: low and high, rich and poor together
row.note: The psalm addresses both low and high and both rich and poor before its teaching about mortality; it makes the commentary's universal insan cross rank boundaries.
The psalm weighs people of high and low estate together and finds them lighter than breath; it joins rank leveling to the commentary's image of universal loss.

row.basis: no favor to prince over poor
row.note: Elihu says God favors neither princes nor rich over poor because all are God's handiwork; noble and lowly share one standing before judgment.

row.basis: rich and poor share their maker
row.note: Proverbs says rich and poor meet under one Maker; this gives the commentary's whole human species a basis independent of social rank.
The Mishnah says humanity began with one person so no one can tell another that his ancestor was greater; it directly interprets shared human origin against pedigree.
Paul says God made every nation from one source; the commentary's insan covers noble and lowly despite claims based on descent.
The verse gives male and female humanity the divine image without a noble lineage; it supplies an account of common human standing.

row.basis: great and small judged by deeds
row.note: The dead, great and small, stand before the throne and are judged by what they have done; rank disappears before the criterion of action.

row.basis: child does not bear parent's guilt
row.note: Ezekiel makes each person's righteousness or wickedness their own; ancestral status does not decide the loss or survival described in the commentary.
Even if Noah were present, Ezekiel says he would save neither son nor daughter but only himself by righteousness; this makes the end of kinship as protection concrete.
John warns hearers not to rely on Abraham as father, since God can raise children for Abraham from stones; a prized ancestry does not settle divine standing.
Those who receive the Word and believe are given the right to become God's children; faith supplies belonging beyond inherited family standing.
The new children of God are born neither from blood nor human will but from God; the verse explicitly displaces pedigree as decisive status.
Paul distinguishes merely physical children from children counted through promise; inherited lineage alone does not establish the standing at issue in the commentary.
Paul calls those of faith Abraham's children; the relationship to an ancestor is redefined by faith rather than birth.
Paul says God repays each person according to deeds; this closely matches the commentary's move from lineage to work.
Paul denies partiality in God's judgment after describing differing deeds; noble or low social identity cannot tilt the verdict.

row.basis: fear God and do right in every nation
row.note: Peter says people in every nation who fear God and do right are acceptable; action and reverence replace descent as a measure of worth.

row.basis: slave and free one in Christ
row.note: Paul says slave and free share one standing in Christ; the commentary's very low freedmen cannot be excluded by their former rank.
Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as more than a slave, a beloved brother; the social valuation of a dependent person is reversed within faith.
Paul calls the slave summoned by the Lord a freedperson of the Lord; the commentary's pairing of freed status with the lowest rank meets a spiritual reversal.
Paul names circumcision, Israelite descent, Benjamin, and Hebrew identity as status credentials; he then assesses that pedigree against faith.
Paul counts his preceding pedigree and religious advantages as loss for Christ; the same human claim to gain becomes loss when measured by faith.
Jesus says the expected sons of the kingdom are thrown into outer darkness; inherited proximity is no guarantee against final loss.
Lazarus, poor at the rich man's gate, is carried to Abraham's side while the rich man dies; low standing in life is reversed at death.
Abraham recalls the rich man's good things and Lazarus's bad things in life while their conditions now reverse; rank and fortune do not settle final worth.

row.basis: خ س ر / Aramaic חסר; table sound correspondence only
row.note: The royal addressee is weighed and found lacking, using Aramaic חסיר; his throne cannot prevent the deficit, a pointed counterpart to universal khusr.

row.basis: God sees heart, not outward stature
row.note: God rejects the human preference for impressive appearance when choosing a king and sees the heart; inner quality overturns rank by appearance.
Jesus identifies whoever does God's will as brother, sister, and mother; enacted obedience replaces ordinary family ties as the bond that counts.
The king identifies acts done for the least of his brothers with acts done for him; treatment of lowly people determines the verdict.
Hebrews says Noah responded in faith to warning, built the ark, and condemned the world; the Noah scene is evaluated by faith rather than the status of his critics.
The epistle calls Noah a herald of righteousness and says God preserved him while bringing the flood on the ungodly; it places righteousness at the center of the Noah story.
Genesis characterizes Noah as righteous and walking with God; this contrasts with the commentary's quoted elite dismissal of Noah's followers as low rank.
Israel's shepherds fail to strengthen weak sheep or seek lost ones; the commentary likewise puts the weak and the lost beside a hierarchy that devalues them.
God vows to seek the lost and strengthen the weak while judging powerful sheep; the verse reunites the commentary's loss, human weakness, and rank reversal.
God announces judgment between fat sheep and lean sheep; strength and rank among the flock become grounds for divine scrutiny rather than privilege.
Jesus says the humbled tax collector goes home justified while the self exalting Pharisee does not; perceived religious rank fails before God.
The wicked remember deriding the righteous person and making him an object of reproach; their contempt parallels the elite's scorn for lowly believers in the commentary.
The wicked admit they treated the righteous person's life as madness and his death as dishonorable; judgment exposes their status based misreading.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The psalm asks why God remembers mortal enosh and then speaks of human honor; this universal, vulnerable human is a useful counterpart to the commentary's all inclusive insan.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The days of enosh are compared with grass; human frailty gives content to the commentary's claim that loss reaches every rank.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: God turns enosh back to dust; the same human category is placed under a fate that levels ancestry and status.

row.basis: ء ن س / Aramaic אנש; table sound correspondence only
row.note: Daniel sees one like a son of enash approaching the Ancient of Days; the Aramaic human designation leads to conferred dominion, a different outcome for a human figure than universal loss.

row.basis: no one can ransom a brother
row.note: The psalm says one person cannot ransom another from death; family solidarity cannot avert the final loss evoked by the commentary's severed kinship.
The psalm says a person in honor does not endure and is like beasts that perish; noble standing does not exempt anyone from loss.
Jeremiah says each person dies for their own iniquity, countering a proverb of inherited guilt; personal conduct displaces family identity in the verdict.

row.basis: God takes no bribe or partial side
row.note: God is called one who shows no partiality and accepts no bribe; the claim of noble birth cannot purchase a favorable judgment.

row.basis: neither favor poor nor defer to great
row.note: The judge must favor neither poor nor great but judge rightly; the verse prevents even rank reversal from becoming a new bias.
Job grounds just treatment of his servants in God's making both parties in the womb; unequal household rank is subordinate to common human origin.

row.basis: ancestors cannot recognize or secure us
row.note: The prayer says Abraham does not know the people and Israel does not acknowledge them, then appeals to God as father; ancestor names cannot themselves guarantee belonging.
The people will again see the distinction between righteous and wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not; the decisive division is conduct.

row.basis: خ س ر / Hebrew חסר; table sound correspondence only
row.note: Proverbs says a giver to the poor will not lack, using חסר; care for lowly people reverses deficiency through an act rather than through social standing.
The maxim calls honorable the one who honors other people; it makes ethical action, rather than noble ancestry, the source of honor.

row.basis: all humanity beloved as image bearers
row.note: The maxim calls humankind beloved because created in God's image; it interprets common humanity as dignity shared by noble and lowly.

row.basis: great and small alike God's concern
row.note: The text says God made both small and great and cares equally for all while rulers face scrutiny; divinely granted rank does not exempt the powerful.
The new priest's standing is described as arising from indestructible life rather than a law of bodily descent; a religious rank is detached from genealogy.

row.basis: Father judges each one's work impartially
row.note: The letter calls God an impartial judge of each person's work; filial language cannot turn family standing into exemption.
Readers are said to have been redeemed from a futile way of life handed down by their ancestors; inheritance itself can transmit what must be left behind.
Jesus predicts a reversal of first and last after teaching about discipleship and wealth; present rank cannot be projected into final standing.
Jesus says many from east and west will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; access to the ancestral banquet is opened beyond inherited rank.
The king says neglect of one of the least was neglect of him; the lowly are a measure of deeds in final judgment.

row.basis: خ س ر / Hebrew חסר; table sound correspondence only
row.note: The speaker says he lacks nothing under the Lord's shepherding, using חסר; the reversal of lack may illuminate khusr, though the psalm concerns present trust rather than collective final loss.
Jesus says those judged worthy of the coming age do not marry; this gives a possible analogy to severed family ties, though it addresses marriage rather than ancestral descent.
Hannah warns the proud against arrogant speech because God weighs actions; the commentary likewise locates distinction in deeds rather than the rank people claim.
Hannah says the Lord makes poor and rich, lowers and raises; noble or low standing is unstable before divine choice.
Hannah says God lifts the poor from dust to sit with princes; the lowest people can receive the highest place.
The psalm says God raises the poor from dust; it reverses the commentary's social description of the lowest people.
God seats the needy with the princes of his people; inherited social distance is overturned.
A foreigner joined to the Lord is told not to say that God will separate him from the people; belonging is opened beyond ancestry.
The Lord addresses eunuchs who choose what pleases him and keep his covenant; a person without descendants can gain divine standing through conduct.

row.basis: name better than sons and daughters
row.note: God promises faithful eunuchs a lasting name better than sons and daughters; this directly reverses the loss of lineage as a measure of worth.
Foreigners who join the Lord, serve him, and keep covenant are included; loyalty and action outrank birth.
God accuses powerful sheep of pushing the weak with flank, shoulder, and horns; this adds the mechanism by which rank harms the weak and lost in the commentary.

row.basis: خ س ر / Hebrew חסר; table sound correspondence only
row.note: The righteous eats to satisfaction while the wicked person's stomach lacks, using חסר; deficiency is distributed by moral standing, not inherited rank.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: Job's friend asks whether mortal enosh can be righteous before God; the cognate human category is placed under a universal moral question.

row.basis: learned outcast precedes ignorant high priest
row.note: The Mishnah's status ladder gives way when a learned person of stigmatized birth outranks an ignorant high priest; acquired fidelity to teaching displaces pedigree.

row.basis: honor measured by fear of God
row.note: Sirach asks which human stock deserves honor and answers in terms of fearing the Lord rather than ancestry; it gives the commentary's rank reversal an explicit criterion.
Wisdom says powerful rulers face strict examination while the lowly may receive mercy; high rank increases accountability instead of securing safety.

row.basis: rulers use their unbelief as test
row.note: The authorities ask whether any ruler or Pharisee has believed in Jesus; they make elite standing a test of truth, like the elite objection to Noah's lowly followers.

row.basis: crowd dismissed as ignorant and cursed
row.note: The authorities call the believing crowd ignorant of the law and cursed; this closely matches discrediting a message by degrading its low status adherents.
Scribes ask why Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners; the objection attacks a teacher through the people who follow and gather around him.
Pharisees and scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them; association with despised people becomes their reason to reject him.
Council members see Peter and John as uneducated ordinary men yet recognize their boldness and connection with Jesus; low standing does not discredit their witness.

row.basis: healed man dismissed as unfit to teach
row.note: The authorities tell the formerly blind man he was born entirely in sin and expel him when he challenges them; presumed low status overrides the truth of his testimony.
Jesus says tax collectors and prostitutes enter God's kingdom ahead of his religious interlocutors; socially disgraced people outrank the prestigious by response to God.
James tells the lowly brother to boast in exaltation; faith gives a rank opposite to his social place.
James tells the rich person to boast in humiliation because wealth fades; high worldly rank cannot protect a person from loss.
Paul names Greek, Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave, and free, then makes Christ central to all; despised ethnic and servile labels cannot set rank in this community.

row.basis: master and slave share impartial judge
row.note: Masters are told to abandon threats because their Master in heaven shows no favoritism; the hierarchy over dependent people is judged by one standard.

row.basis: rich commanded to be rich in works
row.note: The wealthy are instructed to do good and be rich in good works; ethical action replaces possessions as the relevant kind of wealth.
Jesus tells those claiming Abraham as father that true children would do Abraham's deeds; a claimed ancestor must be matched by conduct.
John demands fruit fitting repentance immediately before challenging reliance on Abrahamic descent; conduct supplies the missing criterion for the lineage claim.

row.basis: all have sinned and fall short
row.note: Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory; the universal human condition resembles the commentary's loss of insan before its exception.
Paul immediately says people are justified freely through Christ; this supplies the saving answer to the preceding universal shortfall.

row.basis: all die in Adam, made alive in Christ
row.note: Paul places death on all through Adam and life in Christ; one human lineage shares loss while a new relation changes the outcome.
James calls faith dead when it lacks works; the surah commentary expressly says its exception requires both belief and action.
Believers are described as created in Christ for good works; the commentary's exception likewise joins faith to enacted righteousness.

row.basis: one fate for righteous and wicked
row.note: Qoheleth says the righteous and wicked share the same fate of death; its earthly leveling sharpens the commentary's claim that faith and deeds distinguish people from loss.
Qoheleth says no righteous person on earth does good without sin; it intensifies the commentary's universal statement about humanity before the exception.
Ezekiel says a wicked person who turns from sin and keeps God's statutes shall live; action can change the fate inherited status cannot.
Ezekiel says former righteousness cannot save someone who turns to injustice; even a favorable standing cannot replace continuing conduct.
The psalm orders rescue of the weak and needy from wicked hands; it treats the lowly as people to defend, rather than as a contemptible class.

row.basis: giving to poor as lending to God
row.note: Kindness to the poor is treated as a loan to the Lord who repays; conduct toward lowly people carries divine weight.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The human heart is described as deeply sick, using a form of אנש; the same listed root's weakness sense gives a moral dimension to human vulnerability, though its relation to Arabic insan is uncertain.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: Bildad calls enosh a maggot before God; his harsh image lowers every mortal irrespective of ancestry or social position.
The rabbinic account has Noah's contemporaries challenge his ark building and warning; it adds ridicule to the Noah scene, although it does not say they object to his followers' rank.
Jesus asks what it profits someone to gain the whole world and forfeit life; worldly gain can become the personal loss named in the commentary.

row.basis: rich told not to be haughty
row.note: The rich are told not to set hope on uncertain riches but on God; high material standing offers no sure standing before him.

row.basis: once no people, now God's people
row.note: The letter says its recipients once lacked peoplehood but now are God's people; belonging is conferred beyond inherited status.
Jesus forbids status titles among disciples because they have one teacher and are all siblings; kinship in faith levels rank.

row.basis: redeemed from every people and tribe
row.note: A countless multitude from all nations and tribes stands before the throne; final belonging extends across lineages rather than following one noble stock.
